newsitem.title: USA: Republicans say "retreat" needed to build agenda.
newsitem.headline: Republicans say "retreat" needed to build agenda.

text.p: Republicans need to regroup and develop "a common-sense agenda" to be pursued by the party's congressional majority, party leaders meeting here said Friday.

The Republican National Committee, which includes two delegates from each state as well as other prominent Republicans, proposed holding a "retreat" for the party's congressional and state leaders at some point in the future.
Michigan Gov. John Engler told the delegates that Republicans needed to refocus on a "common-sense agenda" that included tax relief, school choice, and making the streets safer.
"The best defence is a good offence," Engler said.
Republican Party Chairman Jim Nicholson agreed that the party needed to develop its message and what was really wanted by the Republican majority.
He asked for a voice-vote on the retreat proposal, which was met with a resounding "yes."
"We need to get away from our beepers," Engler said.

Earlier this week, an internal fight developed within the party leadership in the House of Representatives, where Speaker Newt Gingrich's authority has come under challenge. Gingrich has come under intermittent criticism from the party's staunch conservatives for caving into the Democrats on certain issues and not providing leadership.

"I have unqualified confidence ... in Newt Gingrich," Nicholson told reporters during a break in the meetings. But Nicholson's support seemed lukewarm when asked whether Gingrich should step aside. "It's way too soon to speculate," he said.
Several Republicans at the meeting commented on current Capitol Hill hearings on alleged campaign finance abuses, and criticised President Bill Clinton for expressing disinterest in the probe.

"Where is your outrage, why haven't you reacted?" Nicholson asked, addressing Clinton. He said as many as 20 proposed witnesses at the hearings have refused to testify, invoking their Fifth Amendment protection against self-incrimination.

David Norcross, chairman of the committee's task force on campaign finance and a delegate from New Jersey, criticised the current limit of $1,000 per contributor for annual contributions. Raising the contribution limits would cut the time spent raising campaign funds sharply, he said.
Norcross also said the Federal Election Commission was incapable of investigating alleged violations of campaign finance laws, and ought to be confined to reporting the on campaign contributions.
